facts.quote: the three early Angkor temples known as the "Roluos group" are located to the north-west of the village of this name

final.notes:
The only disagreement was over facts 1 and 2, about the Roluos River. A Penn Museum Expedition article is a reliable source for both. It calls the Roluos the second most important river system on the Angkor plain. It says the river rises at the foot of the Kulen and flows into the marshes of the Tonle Sap; the page spells it "Tonle Dap", which is a typo. The article also says the river was canalised to supply the moats of Hariharalaya, which is the Roluos area. Tour-operator pages confirm that the river runs past Roluos town towards Kampong Phluk. Taken together, this makes both facts true.

The card describes the settlement itself, so leaving the locality empty is acceptable. Siem Reap province is the correct first-level division. This is the Roluos in Prasat Bakong district, not the Roluos commune in Banteay Meanchey.

facts.quote: Within the hour we reached a stark, cinematically-tilted wooden sign sticking out of a mossy puddle that read Last Water Point
There is an upper route (right hand fork) and lower route (left hand fork) to choose from... it also passes the last watering point at 4130m.
the last stream we cross popularly known as the "last water point", before Kibo Hut

final.notes: Last Water Point (~4,130 m) is on the Horombo–Saddle/Kibo leg of the Marangu Route, inside Kilimanjaro National Park, Kilimanjaro Region (first-level), Tanzania. Locality empty is right for a trail point. Fact 0: National Geographic (Andrew Evans, 2012) describes a wooden sign reading "Last Water Point", so the signpost exists; marked true (current condition not confirmed). Fact 1: Marangu sources name two forks from Horombo, the "upper route" (right) and the "lower route" (left), and put the last watering point on the LOWER route. The card's "upper route" contradicts this established naming, so it is false.

Sources describe it as a stream or water point; none I found confirms a physical signpost, so the 'signposted' claim in fact 0 is unverifiable (the 'waypoint on the Marangu Route' part is true). final.notes: Gasa Tshachu lies on the valley floor by the Mo Chhu, below Gasa. It is about 530 m lower than Gasa Dzong and about a 2-hour climb from it (Windhorse Tours), and about 40 min on foot from the nearest road. So "Gasa" as the locality names the nearest town or dzong settlement, not a town the spring is in. Locality should be empty (open valley), or at most the gewog, which I could not confirm. Region Gasa Dzongkhag is correct, because a dzongkhag is a first-level unit. Fact 1 says "Gasa District" and is accurate (Wikipedia: "hot spring near the bank of the Mo Chhu River in Gasa"). Fact 2: the Mo Chhu part is well supported. "Near Gasa Dzong" is loose (a 2-hour climb) but defensible, so I marked it true. Fact 3: BBS reports several ponds after the October 2023 rebuild following the 2021 flood. The official gasa.gov.bt page was unavailable when I tried it.

That is widely known, but the quoted sentence only confirms the lakeside setting.

facts.quote: Mount Kilimanjaro is a large dormant stratovolcano in Tanzania.
composed of three distinct volcanic cones: Kibo, the highest ... Shira, the lowest at 4,005 m
Uhuru Peak is the highest summit on Kibo's crater rim ... both list the height of Uhuru Peak as 5,895 m (19,341 ft).
it is located in northeastern Tanzania, approximately 20 kilometers (12.4 miles) from the border with Kenya.

final.notes: The mountain is a massif inside Kilimanjaro National Park, so leaving locality empty is correct. Wikipedia's infobox gives the location as "Kilimanjaro Region, Tanzania", which is a first-level region. Sources say northeastern Tanzania; the card's "northern Tanzania" is broadly accurate. For fact 3 the only source with a verbatim quote is a tour operator (Altezza); search results from other sites gave the same ~20 km from the Kenya border.
